To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) a buoyant gravity flow in a rotating fluid is strongly affected by geostrophic motion and (b) a salinity front in a rotating fluid moves away from the source of freshwater discharge.

the penetration of a salinity interface into a rotating fluid depends on vertical diffusion in the Ekman layers and on geostrophic motion, and that the penetration is greatly enhanced by the geostrophic motion if the interface is deep enough.

a salinity front moves away from the wall in a basin with a rotating stratified fluid, the movement of the front is described by the diffusion of the depth of a layer interface, and the diffusivity associated with the antisymmetric part of this diffusion tensor is much greater than that associated with the symmetric part.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the penetration of a salinity (or temperature) front into a rotating fluid in the presence of a sidewall.
the propagation of a salinity interface in a rotating basin.
the penetration of a salinity gradient into a rotating basin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the penetration of a salinity intrusion into a rotating basin is a complex problem that is well described by a simple theory.
a salinity front moves into a rotating basin at a rate determined primarily by the vertical friction and secondarily by the geostrophic motion.
the salinity front penetrates into the basin due to the action of friction in the Ekeman layer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a simple theory with a single parameter (the Ekman layer depth) captures the essence of the observed behavior of a buoyant gravity front penetrating a rotating basin.
the penetration of the front is mainly due to vertical mixing, while the horizontal motion of the front is dominated by the geostrophic effect.

a simple twolayer model can describe the penetration of a salinity gradient in a basin with rotation, and that a salinity front can penetrate into a rotating basin much faster than the Coriolis time scale.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a simple theory with only one ageostrophic effect (vertical friction) captures the essential dynamics of a gravity current penetrating into an ambient fluid rotating in an enclosed basin.
the penetration of the salinity front into the basin is controlled by vertical friction in the Ek man layer.
the penetration of a salinity interface in a rotating basin can be explained with a two-layer theory that only includes friction in the Ekaman layer.
